content: Ovulation is a critical process in the menstrual cycle, during which a mature ovarian follicle ruptures and releases an ovum (also referred to as an oocyte, female gamete, or egg) that is capable of participating in reproduction. This process is not exclusive to humans and also occurs in the estrous cycles of other animals, although the estrous cycle differs significantly from the menstrual cycle in various fundamental ways. The regulation of ovulation is orchestrated by the hypothalamus in the brain, which governs the release of hormones from the anterior pituitary gland. Specifically, luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) play pivotal roles. During the follicular (pre-ovulatory) phase of the menstrual cycle, the ovarian follicle undergoes a series of changes known as cumulus expansion, a process stimulated by FSH. Following this, a small opening called the stigma forms in the follicle, allowing the ovum to exit. Ovulation is triggered by a surge in the levels of FSH and LH released from the pituitary gland. Once ovulation occurs, the ovum travels through the fallopian tubes toward the uterus during the luteal (post-ovulatory) phase. If fertilization by a sperm cell occurs, the ovum may implant in the uterine lining approximately 6 to 12 days later. If fertilization does not occur, the ovum degrades within the fallopian tubes within 24 hours. In humans, the days surrounding ovulation constitute the fertile phase of the menstrual cycle. On average, ovulation occurs on the 14th day of a 28-day menstrual cycle, though this timing can vary, with ovulation commonly occurring between the 10th and 19th days. It is important to note that cycle length alone is not a reliable predictor of the exact day of ovulation. The ovulatory phase, strictly defined, spans the period of hormonal elevation in the menstrual cycle and typically requires no more than 36 hours to complete. This phase is often divided into three stages: periovulatory, ovulatory, and postovulatory. The process of ovulation is preceded by a series of events that take approximately 375 days, or 13 menstrual cycles, to complete. During this time, a large cohort of dormant primordial follicles in the ovary undergoes growth and selection, ultimately resulting in the development of a single preovulatory follicle. Histologically, the preovulatory follicle, also known as a mature Graafian follicle, contains an oocyte arrested in prophase of meiosis I. This oocyte is surrounded by several layers, including corona radiata granulosa cells, mural granulosa cells, a protective basal lamina, and a network of capillaries sandwiched between the theca interna and theca externa cells. The follicle also contains a large fluid-filled cavity called the antrum. A bridge of cumulus oophorus granulosa cells connects the corona-oocyte complex to the mural granulosa cells. These granulosa cells engage in bidirectional communication with the theca cells and the oocyte to support follicular function. Luteinizing hormone (LH) stimulates the theca cells of the preovulatory follicle to secrete androstenedione, which is then converted by mural granulosa cells into estradiol, a form of estrogen. Unlike other phases of the menstrual cycle, the release of estrogen during the late follicular phase has a stimulatory effect on the hypothalamus, promoting the release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). This, in turn, stimulates the production of LH and FSH by the pituitary gland, marking the onset of the periovulatory phase. For ovulation to be successful, the ovum must remain supported by the corona radiata and cumulus oophorus granulosa cells. The cumulus cells undergo a process of proliferation and mucification, known as cumulus expansion. Mucification involves the secretion of a hyaluronic acid-rich matrix that disperses and suspends the cumulus cell network in a sticky substance surrounding the ovum. This network remains with the ovum after ovulation and is essential for fertilization. The proliferation of cumulus cells also increases the volume of antral fluid, causing the follicle to swell to over 20 mm in diameter and form a pronounced bulge on the ovarian surface, referred to as the blister. During the ovulatory phase, a signal transduction cascade initiated by LH leads to the secretion of proteolytic enzymes by the follicle. These enzymes degrade the follicular tissue at the site of the blister, creating an opening called the stigma. The ovum-cumulus complex exits the ruptured follicle through the stigma and enters the peritoneal cavity, where it is captured by the fimbriae at the end of the fallopian tube (oviduct). Once inside the oviduct, the ovum-cumulus complex is propelled toward the uterus by ciliary action. By this stage, the oocyte has completed meiosis I, resulting in two cells: a larger secondary oocyte containing all the cytoplasmic material and a smaller, inactive first polar body. Meiosis II begins immediately but is arrested in metaphase and will only resume upon fertilization. The spindle apparatus for the second meiotic division appears at the time of ovulation. If fertilization does not occur, the oocyte degenerates approximately 24 hours after ovulation. Meanwhile, the uterine lining, or endometrium, reaches its maximum thickness, and the endometrial glands, though non-secretory, are fully developed. In the postovulatory phase, the follicle transforms into the corpus luteum, a steroidogenic structure that produces estrogen and progesterone. These hormones stimulate the endometrial glands to transition from a proliferative to a secretory state, preparing the uterus for potential embryonic implantation. Progesterone also raises basal body temperature by 0.25 to 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.5 to 1 degree Fahrenheit). The corpus luteum continues to support the endometrium for the remainder of the menstrual cycle before degenerating into scar tissue during menstruation if fertilization does not occur. Ovulation can be detected through various signs, including changes in cervical mucus, cervical position, and basal body temperature. Some women also experience secondary fertility signs, such as mittelschmerz (ovulation pain) and heightened olfactory sensitivity. Many women report increased sexual desire in the days leading up to ovulation. Research has even suggested that women may subtly enhance their facial attractiveness during ovulation. Recent studies have challenged the traditional understanding of follicular growth regulation during the menstrual cycle. It is now believed that most women experience two or three waves of follicular development during a typical 28-day cycle, with only the final wave resulting in ovulation. The other waves are anovulatory, characterized by follicular atresia or the absence of a dominant follicle. This phenomenon, similar to follicular waves observed in cows and horses, suggests that the endocrine system may not regulate folliculogenesis as strictly as previously thought. Ovulation can be induced pharmacologically using hormones such as FSH, GnRH, and estradiol, or their synthetic analogs. These agents accelerate folliculogenesis and are commonly used in assisted reproductive technologies for conditions like polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) and oligomenorrhea. Medications such as Clomid, Gonal-F, Follistim AQ, Metformin, Bravelle, Menopur, and Repronex are frequently prescribed for this purpose. However, ovulation-inducing medications carry risks, including a potential link to an increased risk of ovarian carcinoma. Conversely, ovulation can be suppressed for contraceptive purposes. Most hormonal contraceptives target the ovulatory phase of the menstrual cycle, as it is the most critical determinant of fertility. Hormone therapy, including combined oral contraceptive pills containing estradiol and progesterone, mimics the hormonal levels of the menstrual cycle and suppresses ovulation through negative feedback mechanisms. In animals, ovulation mechanisms vary. For example, in camels, ovulation is induced by male pheromones, while in cats and rabbits, it is mechanically triggered by copulation. Chickens ovulate almost daily, and some marsupial species exhibit embryonic diapause, delaying implantation after fertilization.
